Jules Verne. The French author who pioneered the scientific romance and is widely regarded as a father of science fiction. His prolific output spanned submarine adventures, lunar voyages, and extraordinary journeys across and beneath the Earth, marrying scientific extrapolation with page-turning adventure. Verne wrote Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea in 1870, featuring the mysterious submarine Nautilus and the renegade commander Captain Nemo—a work that anticipated submarines and oceanic exploration. He authored Journey to the Center of the Earth in 1864, imagining a subterranean world with prehistoric flora and fauna accessible through volcanic tunnels. Verne created Around the World in Eighty Days in 1873, following the globe-trotting journey of Phileas Fogg—a feat of near-futuristic travel technology and speed. He wrote From the Earth to the Moon in 1865 and continued the narrative with Around the Moon in 1870, imagining lunar voyages in remarkable technical detail, decades before actual spaceflight. Verne produced over sixty novels in his "Extraordinary Voyages" series, spanning science fiction, adventure, and speculative geography. Combined throughout was his meticulous attention to scientific plausibility paired with breathless narrative pacing, creating a template for scientific romance that inspired generations of readers and inventors to imagine the technological future.
